subtype: Approach: small experiments before big moves [Action]
passage: I'm Raghav, and for a year I'd been curious about product management without knowing if I'd enjoy it. Switching tracks on a hunch felt risky, so I asked Nitin, who leads a product team at my company, if I could help on a side project for three months. First I told my manager. Then I blocked Thursday afternoons. Then I took the user-interview notes and a small survey. In month two I wrote my first summary of what customers wanted, and in month three I ran a review meeting myself. By the end I knew I loved the customer side and disliked the long meetings about dates. So I've applied for a research-heavy product role, not the general switch I'd pictured.

qa.q: How long did the side project last?
qa.a: The side project lasted three months.

qa.q: Why did switching tracks on a hunch feel risky to Raghav?
qa.a: Raghav was curious but unsure of liking the work, so a wrong jump felt risky and a cautious trial felt safer.

qa.q: What other approach could Raghav add before applying, and why?
qa.a: Raghav could talk with a few people who already work in product roles about their days, since that shows the parts of the job a short project may not.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Raghav's request?
qa.a: Nitin probably sees a colleague serious enough to test the work in real conditions, and gains some extra help on the project.

grounding: Shows a person trying a three-month side project to test fit for a new track before committing to a switch.

subtype: Approach: small experiments before big moves [Action]
passage:
Supervisor's note, end of the side project, 30 June.
For three months, Sonali, a backend developer from another team, has spent Friday afternoons with our product team as a trial. She wanted to know whether product management fits her before asking for a transfer.
What I observed: she ran four customer interviews, wrote two feature briefs and sat in every prioritisation meeting. She was strong on clear writing and weak at first on saying no to requests; by May she was pushing back well. She also told me honestly that she missed writing code more than she expected.
We talked today. She is not switching yet. She wants one more quarter, focused on data products that mix both. I have agreed and will check in with her manager.
Gurleen

qa.q: How many customer interviews did Sonali run?
How might Sonali have felt on missing code more than she expected?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little torn, learning that product work suited her in some ways but not in others.

qa.q: Why was a three-month trial a better approach than an immediate switch?
qa.a: It let Sonali test the fit and discover she missed coding, without giving up her current role.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's product team be affected by Sonali's Fridays?
qa.a: They got extra help with interviews and briefs, and a developer's view in prioritisation meetings.

grounding: It shows a supervisor's note on a developer who spends three months on a product side project to test fit before switching tracks.

Sunday, 2 March
Month one of my product experiment is done. The deal I made with myself: three months of Thursday afternoons helping Devika's product team with the new onboarding flow. No transfer request until June.
What surprised me: I loved the customer calls. Hearing a shopkeeper in Surat explain why he gave up on our app within two minutes taught me more than a month of tickets. What I hated: the meetings about meetings. Devika says that part is real and doesn't go away.
Score so far: interest 8/10, energy after Thursdays 5/10.
Two more months. I'll decide in June with actual data about myself, not a daydream.
Chetan

qa.q: Who explained why he gave up on the app?
How does Chetan feel about the product work so far?
qa.a: Chetan feels mixed: excited by customer calls but drained by meetings about meetings.

qa.q: What could Chetan watch for in the next two months to make the June decision clearer?
qa.a: Chetan could note which tasks leave energy high or low each Thursday, and ask Devika how much of the job is meetings.

qa.q: How might Devika see Chetan's experiment?
qa.a: Devika gets extra help and can be honest about the hard parts, likely glad the fit is being tested before any transfer.

grounding: It shows someone curious about product management taking a three-month side project with a product team to test fit before switching tracks.
